anomaly_def.Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions and logically deleted index entries because vacuum/cleanup workers cannot keep pace with update-delete churn or long-running snapshots.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Severe competition among sessions for buffer frames, page pins, and lightweight latches, leading to stalls, CPU spin, and inflated wait-event counters on hot pages.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Saturation of the physical storage layer’s bandwidth or IOPS budget, causing elevated read/write latency, deep I/O queues, and database waits dominated by file-I/O events.

Composite behaviour: When these three root causes strike concurrently, the database exhibits runaway bloat of heap and index pages, soaring buffer-busy and page-latch waits, and steadily rising device-level latency. Cleanup processes remain permanently backlogged, checkpoint and background-writer activity increase, and active queries suffer from both latch spin and prolonged I/O waits. Autovacuum or purge workers contend with foreground sessions for the same hot pages, amplifying latch contention, while their flush traffic keeps the storage queue saturated. Administrators observe shrinking buffer-hit ratios despite high memory usage, drastic variance in statement latency, frequent snapshot-too-old or transaction-ID wraparound warnings, and overall throughput collapse even though CPU utilisation appears moderate.

Causal chain: Heavy update/delete workloads create large volumes of dead tuples, inflating page counts and forcing more pages into the buffer pool. This expansion raises the probability that many sessions touch the same root or index pages, intensifying latch contention. The extra dirty pages generated by version churn must eventually be flushed, pushing sustained write rates toward or beyond the storage subsystem’s limits; once the I/O path saturates, checkpoints lengthen and dirty pages remain in cache longer, holding latches and pinning buffer slots. Prolonged I/O waits slow cleanup workers further, allowing even more version buildup. The resulting feedback loop—version bloat → latch pressure → I/O saturation → impaired cleanup—drives a self-reinforcing degradation that can cripple OLTP workloads unless all three layers (vacuuming, buffer management, and storage bandwidth) are addressed together.

entry.official_description: Error updating transaction snapshot version reference for internal storage.
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with a general engine-level execution problem surfaced by the official error catalogue, but its precise trigger must be interpreted together with workload context and surrounding evidence.
entry.solution_guidance: Review the surrounding workload, official description, and engine state to determine whether the issue is rooted in SQL logic, resource pressure, configuration, or environmental instability.
